results.summary: This design implements a digital desk clock that displays hours, minutes, and seconds in 24-hour format. It uses SPI to drive a MAX7219 7-segment display driver because there are not enough output pins to directly control six 7-segment displays. The time can be set using dedicated buttons for hours and minutes, with a fast/slow adjustment mode and a 12-hour mode option. The design requires an external MAX7219 module and a 32.768 kHz reference clock for accurate timekeeping.

This project implements a 32x8 dual-port-read single-port-write RAM using D-type flip-flops, described by the author as a 'really bad implementation' due to its inefficiency. The RAM has two read ports (A and B) and one write port (A), with configurable features such as read buffering, write-through policy, and page selection via configuration bits latched on reset release. It is intended to be tested with standard Tiny Tapeout hardware and an RP2040, and a MicroPython interface is planned. The design is notable for its use of flip-flops instead of dedicated RAM blocks and its flexible read/write policies.

This design implements an 8-bit Concurrent Built-In Logic Block Observer (CBILBO) for memory testing, using shift registers, multiplexers, and feedback logic. It provides a way to observe and control internal memory elements for test purposes. The project includes input and output paths for Tiny Tapeout and supports asynchronous reset. No external hardware is required for testing, and the design is intended to be verified through simulation of its shifting and feedback behavior.

This is an 8-bit CPU based on the SAP-1 architecture, developed as part of a university course. It includes a control unit, program counter, instruction register, 16-byte memory, arithmetic logic unit with flags, accumulator, and output register. The CPU can execute a small instruction set and provides outputs for the accumulator and flags. It is intended for educational purposes and can be tested by providing opcodes and observing outputs.

This is the MIPS processor core example from the Weste & Harris textbook, written by Max Yi and David Harris. It implements a subset of the MIPS architecture with separate memory address, read, and write interfaces. The design requires an external program store to function. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it needs a program store and that testing should be done 'carefully'.

This is a simple Verilog test project that accumulates the value on the dedicated input pins into an internal register every clock cycle. The least significant bits of the accumulated value are output on the dedicated output pins, while the most significant bits are output on the bidirectional pins. It is intended as a basic demonstration and requires switches on inputs and LEDs on outputs for testing. The design is minimal and serves as a template or experiment.

This project implements a 4-bit multiplier that takes two 4-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit product. It uses a manual structural design with AND gates and full adders to compute the multiplication. The design was created for a digital logic course lab and includes a Python test script for verification. No external hardware is required.

This design implements a basic oscilloscope and signal generator on an ASIC, using an external ADC, DAC, FRAM, and HDMI Pmod. It samples input signals, buffers them in FRAM, and displays waveforms on an HDMI screen, with the display rotated 90 degrees due to memory constraints. The signal generator uses direct digital synthesis to produce sine, square, triangle, and sawtooth waves, and the oscilloscope supports trigger functionality. The design requires multiple external Pmods and outputs settings via UART.

This project implements a small Configurable Logic Block (CLB) with a 3-input Look-Up Table (LUT3). It takes two 8-bit inputs: one for the LUT configuration and control signals, and another for the boolean function arguments. The output is the evaluation of the configured boolean function. The design can be tested by setting the LUT to implement a NAND3 function and using switches and LEDs for input and output.

This project implements a histogramming unit, but the documentation is essentially empty, providing no details on its functionality, interface, or usage. The pin names are generic and do not indicate specific behavior. It is not possible to determine how the design works or how to test it from the available information.
